# Finite-plane zero faces, codimension, and the one-dimensional no-defect consequence

This is a bounded consequence of `candidate 8ba63f3af7e6943f`. It retains the exact tilted rows and does not infer an ordinary depth payment or identify their original-volume means.

## 1. Statement

Let K be a positive d-dimensional compact convex body and

    L=min_(1<=i<=m) A_i>=0 on K,

where the A_i are finite affine functions. Suppose L is positive on int K and

    integral_K 1/L < infinity.                         (1)

Then every nonempty zero face `K intersect {A_i=0}` has affine dimension at most d−2. In particular the zero set of L is a finite union of exposed faces of dimension at most d−2 and has zero (d−1)-dimensional surface measure. For d=1 the zero set is empty, so L is strictly positive on the whole closed interval K.

Only necessity is asserted in arbitrary convex bodies: the dimension of a zero face alone need not determine the integrability rate of 1/L near that face.

## 2. The facet divergence argument

Every A_i is nonnegative on K since A_i>=L. If A_i were identically zero on K, positivity on int K would fail. A nonempty zero face therefore lies in a genuine supporting hyperplane.

Suppose its dimension were d−1. After a rigid coordinate change write

    A_i(x',t)=a t,  a>0,  K subset {t>=0}.

The zero face contains a positive (d−1)-ball D in its relative interior. Choose an interior point `(x_0,b)` with b>0. The convex hull of D and that point is contained in K. Its section at height t, 0<t<b/2, is a translate of `(1-t/b)D`, with (d−1)-volume at least `2^(−d+1)|D|`. Hence

    integral_K 1/L >= integral_K 1/A_i
       >=[2^(−d+1)|D|/a] integral_0^(b/2) dt/t
       =infinity,

contradicting (1). For d=1 use the same argument with D a point and its zero-dimensional volume equal to one; it is precisely the divergence of the reciprocal of an affine function at an interval endpoint. This proof does not require K to be a polytope or its other boundary points to be smooth.

## 3. Application to the actual limiting rows

In the row-limit theorem, sampled fibers K_z^j converge to positive K_z, and the finite-plane representatives converge uniformly on a common compact set to L. The exact limiting measure is

    nu=dm/(M L)+zeta,
    zeta>=0,  support(zeta) subset {L=0}.

Its mass is bounded by the reciprocal lower bound on the old source values. Thus (1) holds separately in every sampled fiber. Section 1 applies to each restriction `A_i(z,.)`.

Consequently all possible defect mass lies on the finite union of sampled zero faces of continuous codimension at least two. These sets are null for the ordinary sampled surface measures. This localization is stronger than merely saying that the defect lies on the boundary, but it does not make the defect zero for d>=2. In particular a limiting surface stress does not directly detect this defect by absolute continuity with respect to the surface measure.

## 4. No inverse-volume defect in continuous dimension one

When d=1, every limiting sampled interval has L>0 at both endpoints and throughout. There are only finitely many bases. Therefore

    m_0=min_(z in P,x in K_z) L(z,x)>0.

Continuity of the finite-plane L on the common ambient compact set gives a neighborhood of the limiting sampled intervals where L>=m_0/2. Hausdorff convergence places all current sampled intervals in that neighborhood for large j, and uniform L_j convergence gives `L_j>=m_0/4` on them.

Regard all measures on the fixed disjoint union of a common continuous bounding interval, one copy for each sampled base. Their densities are

    g_j(z,x)=1_(K_z^j)(x)/(M_j L_j(z,x)).

They are eventually uniformly bounded. The indicators converge Lebesgue-almost everywhere by interval endpoint convergence, M_j tends to M, and L_j tends uniformly to L. Dominated convergence proves

    ||g_j−1_(K_z)/(M L)||_(L1)=0.

Thus the inverse-volume measures converge in total variation, are uniformly integrable, and zeta=0. The limiting tilted martingale has target exactly dm/(M L). Every surviving positive-weight row is likewise dominated by a fixed multiple of these densities and has no boundary concentration. No assertion is made about zero-weight rows retained only as bookkeeping labels.

This conclusion uses the actual bounded total inverse mass and the finite-plane limit, not just bounded L maxima or source interiority separately.

## 5. The codimension threshold is sharp in every d>=2

Take the exact truncated-triangle construction from
`candidate 1b1d5e313c1943d1`, and form its Cartesian product with `[0,1]^(d−2)`. For d=2 the extra factor is a point of volume one. Keep the affine parameter independent of the new variables. All normalization integrals, source-value bounds, and one-row contact identities are unchanged, while the extra source coordinates are 1/2.

The bodies converge to

    K={x,y>=0, x+y<=1} times [0,1]^(d−2),
    L=exp(1/2)(x+y).

The limiting inverse-volume measure is exactly

    2 exp(−1/2) [ dx dy/(x+y) + (log 2) delta_(0,0) ]
                    tensor Lebesgue_([0,1]^(d−2)).

Its nonzero defect is supported on the exposed zero face

    {(0,0)} times [0,1]^(d−2),

which has dimension d−2. For d>=3 this supplies a non-atomic defect on a positive-dimensional zero face. The original-volume reweighted rows still converge to uniform volume without this defect. The source is not deepest and no physical stationary minimum is asserted; this is a sharp calibration of the row-limit hypotheses only.

## 6. Exact scope

The new conclusion is a degeneracy classification: continuous dimension one rules out every inverse-volume boundary defect in this finite-plane contact limit; higher dimensions confine such defects to continuous codimension at least two, and that bound is sharp. It neither removes those higher-dimensional defects using deepestness nor promotes the tilted martingale to an original-volume martingale.
